Article Title: 'Punjabis don't like politics over dead': CM Mann counters Rahul over Gulzar Singh's suicide
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann on Wednesday countered Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi for pinning the blame for Gulzar Singh's suicide on Aam Aadmi Party-led Punjab government, advising him not to "do politics over dead bodies."In a social media post on X, Mann said that all the accused have been caught by the police based on identification by the family."Rahul Gandhi ji, don't do politics over dead bodies; Punjabis don't like this kind of politics," Mann said.Mann also shared a video in which a Congress leader was seen facing villagers' protest."Look here, when Congress leaders went to the victim's village and still tried to indulge in this dirty politics, the people chased them away from there," the chief minister said."In this case, all the accused have already been caught by the police based on identification by the family. The Akali, BJP, and Congress governments have been responsible for spreading drugs in Punjab. In my government, no drug smuggler will be spared," Mann said.Earlier in the day, Rahul accused the AAP of "crushing those who question" the Punjab government after Gulzar - a villager in Punjab - died by suicide following alleged pressure to apologise for publicly questioning the state's finance minister over the drug menace in the state.In a social media post on X, Rahul said Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann should immediately demand his minister Harpal Singh Cheema's resignation and ensure an independent and impartial investigation."A dangerous pattern is emerging in Punjab's AAP government - if you question government failures, the response will come in the form of threats and torture," Rahul said."Gulzar Singh ji, from the Dalit community, who had to watch his son fall victim to drugs, asked the finance minister just this much: why has the government failed so miserably in stopping the drug trade? For just this, he was tortured and humiliated so much, pressured so intensely to apologise, that he consumed poison. Wandering from one hospital to another, without access to treatment, he ultimately lost the battle for his life," he added.He said the government's job is to answer to the people, "not to crush those who ask questions"."The government's job is to answer to the people, not to crush those who ask questions. May Gulzar Singh ji's family get justice as soon as possible. The chief minister should immediately demand the finance minister's resignation and ensure an independent and impartial investigation, with his name registered in the FIR," the Congress leader said.A controversy erupted after a 47-year-old man, Gulzar Singh, from Sangrur allegedly died by suicide, with his family claiming that he was asked to apologise and subjected to casteist slurs for questioning finance minister Harpal Singh Cheema over the "unabated" supply of 'chitta' in his area at an event on September 6.Singh died on Monday night after allegedly consuming poison, his family members said.A purported video of Gulzar's last moments surfaced in which he spoke about questioning the finance minister, prompting opposition parties to demand the resignations of Cheema as well as Mann.Punjab Police set up a special investigation team (SIT), led by an officer of additional director general of police rank, in connection with the suicide incident.Following a complaint by Gulzar's family, five villagers - Baljit Singh, Sukhdev Singh, Vicky Singh, Gona Singh and Baljinder Kaur - have been booked under Section 108 (abetment of suicide) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and relevant sections of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, according to the FIR.
Article Summary: Rahul Gandhi accused the AAP of "crushing those who question" the Punjab government. Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann said that all the accused have been caught by the police based on identification by the family. A controversy erupted after a 47-year-old man, Gulzar Singh, from Sangrur, allegedly died by suicide.

Article Title: BJP announces month-long ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ to mark PM Modi’s 25 years in public service

Campaign to begin on PM Modi’s birthday

NEW DELHI: The BJP will launch a month-long ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ on September 17 to mark PM Modi completing 25 years in public service, with programmes ranging from blood donation and cleanliness drives to exhibitions, seminars and welfare-scheme camps across the country.The campaign will continue until October 17. October 7 will mark 25 years since PM Modi took oath as Gujarat chief minister in 2001.Announcing the campaign at the BJP headquarters in New Delhi on Wednesday, party national president Nitin Nabin said, “Today, we have gathered here to discuss the 'Seva Sankalp Abhiyan'. On October 7, 2026, the Prime Minister Narendra Modi will complete 25 years of public service, a journey that began when he assumed office as the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001. Over the past 25 years, he has steadfastly continued this journey of service, embracing the mantra of transitioning from public service to service of the nation. ”The campaign will start on September 17, PM Modi’s birthday, which the BJP observes as ‘Seva Diwas’.“We will begin the programme with a blood donation camp. On September 17, we will organise the 'Ashirwad Ka Diya' programme. On October 2, we will organise a cleanliness drive, as we do every year,” Nabin said.An inaugural programme titled ‘Ashirbadar Banti’ (Lamp of Blessings) will also be held on September 17.BJP national general secretary Vinod Tawde has been appointed national convener of the campaign. A seven-member team comprising a minister, an organisational general secretary and five senior leaders will be formed in every state to coordinate the programmes.The party will hold photo and digital exhibitions tracing PM Modi’s 25-year political journey and focusing on his governance record, development initiatives and welfare schemes.Seminars and intellectual forums on good governance, development and Antyodaya are also planned, along with interactions with young people and other sections of society. Special camps will spread awareness about welfare schemes run by the Centre and state governments and the benefits available under them.“I believe that it is the BJP's responsibility to take this message of public service and dedication to the people,” Nabin said.Nabin used the announcement to contrast India’s economic position before PM Modi became Prime Minister in 2014 with the present.“When he took over the leadership of the country, India was facing policy paralysis and was being referred to as one of the 'Fragile Five' economies. Today, India is the fastest-growing major economy in the world,” he said.“There was a time when the atmosphere at that time was one of despair and darkness. Our economy was seen as part of the Fragile Five. But today, India stands out as the world's fastest-growing economy,” Nabin said.He also said India’s stature on the global stage had risen under the PM Modi-led government.Turning to young people, Nabin said PM Modi had sought to replace what he described as an atmosphere of despair with hope after 2014.“There was a time when the youth of the country were immersed in an atmosphere of despair. It was the honourable Prime Minister who, since 2014, took up the task of placing them in an environment of hope and optimism,” he said.Nabin cited the expansion of India’s startup ecosystem as part of that shift.“Through startups and unicorns, India has today become the third-largest startup nation in the world. In startups and unicorns, our youth have come forward and emerged as job givers and not just job seekers,” he said.He also referred to Khelo India and Fit India while speaking about opportunities for young people.Women-led development will also form part of the BJP’s account of PM Modi’s tenure.“The Prime Minister spoke about Women-led Development, and the journey that began under his leadership with Beti Bachao-Beti Padhao has today reached the Lakhpati Didi milestone,” Nabin said.He also referred to the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam and the government’s efforts to increase women’s participation in policymaking.Nabin said the government had also sought to change the way border settlements were viewed.“There was a time when border villages were called India's last villages. They changed this perception and started calling them India's first villages. This has not only brought changes in the lives of ordinary people, but has also altered people's outlook towards these communities,” he said.Nabin traced PM Modi’s development record to Gujarat, citing work on the Narmada project and the Vibrant Gujarat initiative.“Gujarat's growth became a development model that other states could aspire to emulate,” Nabin said.He also referred to the government’s campaign against Naxalism and said PM Modi’s record should not be viewed only through economic or physical development.“Under PM Modi's leadership, India's progress has not been limited to material development; our cultural identity and heritage have also been strengthened,” he said.Nabin cited the Ram Mandir and Kashi Vishwanath while discussing the government’s emphasis on cultural heritage.“From the Ram Mandir to Kashi Vishwanath, he has worked to preserve, restore, and develop the country's rich cultural heritage,” he said.Describing PM Modi’s political journey, Nabin said, “His journey began as an ordinary party worker, and today, he has advanced the nation's progress as its 'Pradhan Sevak'. This has been made possible solely through his clear vision, firm resolve, and continuous efforts to bring about qualitative changes in society and transform lives.”PM Modi took oath as Gujarat’s 14th chief minister on October 7, 2001. He served as chief minister for nearly 13 years before moving to national politics and becoming Prime Minister in 2014.
Article Summary: BJP to launch month-long ‘Seva Sankalp Abhiyan’ nationwide to mark 25 years of PM Modi’s parliamentary political journey. Campaign to begin on September 17 to mark PM Modi's birthday, with programmes ranging from blood donation and cleanliness drives to exhibitions, seminars and welfare-scheme camps.

NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday condemned strikes by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabian oil and civilian facilities, saying that such attacks undermine regional security."India condemns attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, especially the targeting of civilian and economic facilities. Attacks that undermine regional security and stability and threaten freedom of navigation in the Bab-el-Mandeb were unacceptable," ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in response to a media query.Jaiswal’s remarks came as the Houthis, the Yemen-based rebel group, targeted Saudi oil facilities and other civilian infrastructure on Tuesday, raising widespread concerns over a further escalation of the conflict in the Middle East.The attacks on Saudi Arabia came as the US intensified its economic sanctions against Iran.As many as 73 people were wounded in a wave of Houthi attacks that targeted “civilian and economic facilities” in the Saudi Arabian cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait.The strikes came hours after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in Yemen’s northern Jawf province. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others wounded in the strike in the city of Hazem.Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, along with large parts of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognised government into exile.A Saudi-led coalition, which included the United Arab Emirates, intervened the following year in an effort to restore the government to power.Tensions between the US allies Saudi Arabia and the UAE escalated earlier this year as their partnership in Yemen’s war deteriorated, ultimately prompting the UAE to withdraw from the conflict.The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed Yemen to the brink of famine.
Article Summary: India condemns attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, especially the targeting of civilian and economic facilities. Attacks that undermine regional security and stability and threaten freedom of navigation in the Bab-el-Mandeb were unacceptable. strikes came hours after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in Yemen's northern Jawf province.

Article Title: Why Vijay's gold ring scheme may miss its September 15 launch
Article Text:
Under Vijay's gold ring scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600.

What is the gold ring scheme?

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay's gold ring scheme, which was scheduled to be launched on September 15, shall be deferred from its expected date. The announcement comes as the CM prepares for his first official overseas visit to London. Vijay is set to meet European industrialists during the visit and pitch Tamil Nadu as an investment destination.Vijay will leave Chennai for London via Dubai on Wednesday night and is expected to stay in the UK capital for a few days. He will travel on an Emirates Airlines passenger flight.During the visit, Vijay is expected to invite European companies to set up businesses in Tamil Nadu and seek fresh investment commitments for the state. Senior officials from the industries and finance departments are also expected to travel to London. Some may leave ahead of the chief minister to prepare for his meetings with prospective investors.The visit comes soon after the ‘Vettri Tamil Nadu Investment Conclave 2026’, where the state government announced investment commitments worth Rs 1,02,514 crore through 104 memorandums of understanding (MoUs).Security and protocol arrangements for Vijay’s departure are also being finalised.A high-level Advance Security Liaison meeting is reportedly scheduled at Chennai’s old airport on Wednesday to review the arrangements.Vijay’s London visit also comes amid key political developments in Tamil Nadu. Before leaving for the UK, he is scheduled to chair a second alliance coordination meeting at the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam headquarters in Panaiyur.The meeting is expected to discuss the structure of the ruling alliance and post-poll coalition arrangements. A Common Minimum Programme is also on the agenda, along with discussions on a steering committee and an official name for the alliance.Invitations have reportedly been sent to all alliance partners, including Congress, VCK, IUML, MDMK, CPI and CPM. Congress, VCK, IUML and MDMK have confirmed their attendance, while the Left parties are likely to stay away.Vijay had announced the one-gram gold ring scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election. The initiative was planned as a symbolic gift to newborns and draws on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’.Under the scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600.“Through this scheme, the government assumes the role of the maaman (uncle) for every child born in its institutions, presenting a gold ring as an enduring token of welcome,” a government order said.The scheme was originally scheduled to be launched on September 15, which coincides with the birth anniversary of former chief minister C N Annadurai.It will have retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday. The government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of the child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.The state has allocated around Rs 755.83 crore annually for the scheme, which will cover all newborns delivered at government institutions. There will be no restriction based on birth order and no gender-based discrimination.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings and supply them based on annual requirements. A project and programme management unit will also be established to oversee implementation and monitoring.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries each year, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or about 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The scheme is open to Tamil Nadu residents whose children are delivered at government institutions. Mothers will have to submit proof of residence, with documents such as ration cards, voter identity cards, Aadhaar, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates accepted.The government said the initiative was intended to combine cultural significance with public healthcare.“Gold carries profound cultural and emotional resonance in Tamil Nadu. Gifting gold to a newborn celebrates the baby’s arrival, honours the mother’s noble journey and transforms public health delivery into a source of immense community pride,” the order said.
Article Summary: Under Vijay's scheme, every newborn delivered at a government health facility will receive a one-gram gold ring. At the current gold rate, the ring is worth around Rs 13,600. Vijay is set to meet European industrialists during the visit and pitch Tamil Nadu as an investment destination.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Wednesday took cognisance of Greater Noida executive magistrate's notice to a 2nd year law student for participating in a protest led by Cockroach Janata Party.Though the notice was withdrawn, the apex court said that it is a serious matter as its September 1 pan-India direction barred action against students.According to the Live Law, the matter was brought to the attention of a bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant."How could a magistrate dare to issue notice? We made clear no coercive action against any student! No magistrate could violate that order," CJI said.This comes a day after Allahabad high court reprimanded Noida DM Medha Roopam for imposing the National Security Act on Delhi University student activist Akriti Chaudhary, saying that errant bureaucrats could reduce Uttar Pradesh to an "Orwellian dystopia" and reminded civil servants that their loyalty lies with the Constitution and not the political executive.A division bench of Justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Achal Sachdev observed that bureaucrats and police officers enjoy immense powers because they are entrusted with protecting the constitutional rights, dignity and welfare of citizens."They must remember that their loyalty is towards the Constitution and not the political executive," the court said.The 15-page order, made public days after the court quashed the NSA detention and awarded Rs 5 lakh compensation to Chaudhary on Sept 2, contains sharp criticism of the Gautam Budh Nagar administration and police for invoking the stringent preventive detention law against a student activist without adequate material.Warning against abuse of authority, the bench observed that when officials disregard their constitutional oath, they risk being perceived as "an oppressive vestige of the British Empire", creating conditions for civil unrest. "It shall not be long before the errant in the bureaucracy reduce the State of Uttar Pradesh to an Orwellian Dystopia," the court remarked.The bench was particularly critical of Gautam Budh Nagar DM Medha Roopam, who had approved the NSA detention.It held that where the police dossier contained only allegations and no credible supporting material, the district magistrate was expected to scrutinise the records threadbare before invoking the extraordinary powers available under the NSA.Chaudhary, a 24-year-old history graduate, was arrested in connection with cases arising from a workers' protest in Noida in April 2026. The UP Police invoked the NSA against her and activist-journalist Satya Verma on May 13. They were among activists arrested in cases related to the protest seeking higher wages.
Article Summary: Supreme Court took cognisance of Greater Noida executive magistrate's notice to a 2nd year law student for participating in a protest led by Cockroach Janata Party. This comes a day after Allahabad high court reprimanded Noida DM Medha Roopam for imposing National Security Act on Delhi University student activist Akriti Chaudhary.

Article Title: Building collapses to fires, 33k died in 5 years from 2020
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 33,000 people died across the country in incidents involving building collapses, fires and falls into pits and manholes, according to govt data. Most of these deaths occurred in urban areas, pointing to serious gaps in civic governance and enforcement of safety regulations.The actual numbers will be significantly higher as data on road deaths within municipal limits – many on account of potholes – and those due to contaminated water are unavailable.The data taken from reports of National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) show that thousands of deaths every year are linked to accidents that are largely preventable and often occur due to poor upkeep of public infrastructure, unsafe buildings and non-compliance with safety regulations. There are no specific data on deaths due to consumption of contaminated water and unhygienic conditions.While recent incidents in Delhi, including those in Satya Niketan, Hauz Rani, Palam and Vivek Vihar have caught the attention of people, instances of parts of Gurgaon and Delhi getting flooded and accumulation of piles of garbage are clear indicators of how municipal governance has deteriorated.“There is a lack of will to address the issues and no one wants to take responsibility.Every corporator or councillor, municipal officer and mayor needs to take responsibility. In every budget, mayors must inform people what they have done, where they have failed and what they would do. Accountability at each level is necessary,” said former urban development secretary M Ramachandran.PSN Rao, dean of School of Planning and Architecture, Delhi said municipal authorities only need to follow the law and enforce rules that are already laid down. “How many municipal commissioners tour different parts of cities? It’s the duty of municipal officers to carry out regular inspections to identify dangerous buildings and take necessary action. There is no alternative to strict enforcement. When there is a red signal, you must stop; else there will be an accident.It’s as simple as that,” he added.A retired civil servant who worked in the urban development ministry and in top positions in states said that there is lack of supervision and monitoring down the line. “There is adequate manpower. Across cities you will find municipal officers knocking at the door when one starts any construction work. So, there is no shortage of hands for monitoring purposes. ‘Fish rots from the head’, as the Japanese saying goes, and things must start from the top,” he said.Experts and former officials who have worked in the sector also stressed that govt’s push for ease of construction and deregulation must follow a balanced approach. “The distinction between deregulating to increase economic activity and deregulation that leads to collapse of civic order is a fine one and has been lost in the rush to deregulate everything. Officers are unable to draw the line and have stopped attending to routine work under the guise of deregulation. An important side-effect has been de-skilling as they are no longer able to decide and act,” one of them said.
Article Summary: Between 2020 and 2024, nearly 33,000 people died across the country in incidents involving building collapses, fires and falls into pits and manholes. Most of these deaths occurred in urban areas, pointing to serious gaps in civic governance and enforcement of safety regulations. Data on road deaths within municipal limits and those due to contaminated water are unavailable.

minister said he had personally visited Kurali, Kharar and Nangal over the past 10 days to review the campaign on the ground and interact with sanitation workers.The department will conduct a detailed analysis of the campaign after September 12, including photographic evidence of garbage vulnerable points that have been permanently eliminated, Bains said.

Article Title: 'Festivals are inclusive': Amruta Fadnavis opposes VHP call to bar Muslims from Navratri events

NEW DELHI: Amruta Fadnavis , wife of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis , said there was nothing wrong with Muslims participating in Navratri and other festivals, after the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) called for Muslims to be barred from the upcoming Navratri festivities, a demand endorsed by state minister Nitesh Rane.“Festivals are inclusive, and there is nothing wrong with a Muslim person attending the celebrations. If a Muslim also comes and enjoys the festival properly, I do not see anything wrong with it,” Amruta Fadnavis told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday, PTI reported.Her remarks came in response to a question on Rane’s comments. On Monday, Rane, a BJP colleague of Devendra Fadnavis, backed the VHP, alleging that cases of “love jihad” tend to increase during such festivals. He also called for attendees to undergo identity checks and recite the Hanuman Chalisa before being allowed entry to Navratri events.“Love jihad” is a term used by right-wing activists to allege that Muslim men lure women, mostly from the Hindu community, into relationships with the aim of converting them to Islam.Last week, the VHP announced that Muslims would not be allowed to enter ‘garba’ and ‘dandiya’ venues across Maharashtra during Navratri, which begins on October 11.The VHP has also issued “guidelines” for organisers to verify participants’ identities at Navratri ‘garba’ and ‘dandiya’ events by checking their Aadhaar cards and applying ‘tilak’ on their foreheads.
Article Summary: Amruta Fadnavis said there was nothing wrong with Muslims participating in Navratri and other festivals. The Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) has called for Muslims to be barred from the upcoming festivities. State minister Nitesh Rane backed the VHP, alleging that cases of “love jihad” tend to increase during such festivals.

NEW DELHI: Total receipts by BJP's central party headquarters during the last round of assembly polls in Bengal, Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry stood at Rs 1,472.8 crore, as per the party's election expenditure statements for Assam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry submitted to the Election Commission.The party's closing balance rose to Rs 7,627.2 crore upon the completion of elections on May 6, 2026, compared to Rs 6,722.6 crore on March 15, 2026.BJP, including the party's central headquarters and the relevant state and district units, spent a total Rs 160 crore on the assembly elections in Assam, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry. The election expenditure statements for the other two states of West Bengal and Kerala are yet to be made public by EC.As per BJP's election expenditure statements for Assam, the party spent Rs 76.7 crore on general party propaganda, which included Rs 23.1 crore spent by its central unit, and another Rs 19.5 crore spent on candidates.While Rs 27.3 crore was spent on travel expenses of star campaigners in Assam, Rs 37 crore was on advertisements, Rs 8.9 crore on publicity materials and Rs 2.3 crore on other expenses by the state unit. A total lump sum of Rs 19.4 crore was paid to candidates and Rs 16.7 lakh spent on publishing criminal antecedents of candidates. In TN, BJP authorised a total spend of Rs 44.5 crore for general party propaganda. Another Rs 7 crore was spent on candidates.In its expenditure statement released earlier for the same set of elections, Congress had declared a total spend of Rs 248.6 crore.
Article Summary: Total receipts by BJP's central party headquarters during the last round of assembly polls in Bengal, Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry stood at Rs 1,472.8 crore. Article Title: Channi vs Warring: Why Sachin Pilot may be Congress's best bet in Punjab
Article Text:

Why Congress was forced to budge

Why Sachin Pilot

Punjab Congress working president welcomed Sachin Pilot’s appointment, saying it will help iron out differences within the state unit.

Baghel gone. Will Warring be next?

Congress has a lot at stake

Punjab could shape Pilot's Rajasthan future

NEW DELHI: The Congress leadership last week finally responded to 'Mayday' calls from Punjab rebels and brought in Sachin Pilot , replacing Bhupesh Baghel , to prevent a crash landing of the deeply fractured state unit ahead of the assembly elections early next year.Months of open infighting between Charanjit Singh Channi, the former chief minister leading the rebel camp, and Raja Warring, the state unit chief, not just embarrassed the Congress but also threatened to derail its 2027 campaign.Before being put in the driver's seat in Punjab, Pilot was in charge of Chhattisgarh, where Baghel remains a key Congress leader and former chief minister.The Congress had sent former Chhattisgarh chief minister Bhagel to Punjab in February this year to defuse the brewing Channi vs Warring crisis in the state unit. Ironically, as things turned out, Baghel faced resistance and became part of the crisis, with the Channi camp openly accusing him of siding with Warring. More so, since July, after the party’s central leadership decided to ignore Channi’s claim for the top post in the state and announced that it would continue with Warring as state Congress president.With several senior state leaders backing Channi, the fight turned ugly and Baghel became ineffective.Congress meetings in the districts saw open “Go back Baghel” chants from Channi supporters, taking the infighting to the streets and embarrassing the top leadership.So, while the ruling Aam Aadmi Party was already in full election mode with chief minister Bhagwant Mann at the centre of its campaign, the Congress was still struggling to get its senior leadership to sit across the table.Not just the AAP, even the BJP and the Akalis had their house in order and were planning their electoral moves on the ground. With the party's 2027 campaign failing to take off under Baghel, the Congress was forced to budge and turn to Pilot.The Congress decision to send Pilot to Punjab, while ironic, may still be the best bet for the leadership. Sachin Pilot, during his years in the Congress, has seen enough internal wars to know how quickly a fight over one post can turn into a larger battle over leadership, political space and, of course, eventually the chief minister's chair.Throwback to Rajasthan, where he spent years at the centre of a similar leadership tussle with senior leader Ashok Gehlot. Pilot brings something the Congress needs badly right now: the experience of being at the centre of a difficult internal power struggle.Pilot has led the Rajasthan unit, worked closely with the high command, weathered the bitter internal battle, survived the fallout and then rebuilt his position within the Congress.He was appointed Rajasthan Congress chief in 2014, after the party's abysmal performance in the 2013 assembly election. Over the next four years, he emerged as one of the key faces of the party's rebuilding effort before Congress returned to power in 2018. That victory, however, did not give him the chief minister's chair.Ashok Gehlot became chief minister, while Pilot was made deputy chief minister and continued as PCC president. While both sides got something, the arrangement never really settled the rivalry between Gehlot and Pilot.By 2020, those differences exploded into an open rebellion.Pilot left Jaipur with a group of MLAs and challenged the Gehlot government. Congress responded by removing him as deputy chief minister and state president. The Gehlot camp even accused him of working with the BJP. A truce was eventually worked out, and Pilot stayed with Congress.But he never quite returned to the position he had occupied before and has been on the sidelines ever since. He remained a prominent face in the party and was later given charge of Chhattisgarh, but his role in Rajasthan remained limited.It is interesting how, in Rajasthan, Pilot was the leader asking the Congress high command to listen to a dissatisfied camp. In Punjab, he now has to convince dissatisfied leaders to accept the high command's decisions and work together.That may be why Congress believes he is best suited for the job.But will Pilot’s appointment end the crisis in the Punjab unit?Channi's supporters had demanded Warring be removed as Punjab Congress chief, and the Jalandhar MP be declared Congress’s chief ministerial face for the 2027 assembly polls. The Congress has not accepted either of the two demands. So, while Channi has not made any significant gains, Warring has been left wondering if he will be the next to be axed.Warring was picked up to lead and rebuild the Punjab unit after the Congress was decimated in the 2022 assembly polls. Channi, who was the chief minister then, led the Congress to its worst-ever performance in the state. The Congress not just lost its government to AAP but was also reduced to 18 seats in the 117-member assembly.The leadership tussle between the two had been brewing for quite some time. But as is the Congress’s wont, the party kept dilly-dallying on the issue for nearly 4 years. Finally, when the Congress did take a decision, it ended up opening deep faultlines.For now, both camps have welcomed his appointment. Warring said Pilot's energy and dynamism would "for sure" add to the vigour of the party ahead of the crucial polls, while Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, a close associate of Channi, said Pilot's experience, leadership and connect with the people would give new strength and momentum to the Congress in Punjab.Punjab Congress working president Raj Kumar Verka hopes that under Pilot’s leadership all state leaders would come together. "Pilot knows all leaders of Punjab, and they also have confidence in him," said Verka.For Pilot, this may be his first real test. If party leadership decides to keep Warring, he has to get Channi, Randhawa and other leaders to fall in line. If Warring goes, he has to make sure one problem is not replaced by the other.The Congress, which remains the main challenger for now, cannot afford this infighting because Punjab is one of the states where it still has a real chance. There is anti-incumbency against the Bhagwant Mann-led AAP government.In 2022, AAP swept 92 of the 117 assembly seats, while Congress was reduced to 18. But the 2024 Lok Sabha election brought some relief for the grand old party. The Congress won seven of Punjab's 13 seats, compared with AAP's three, showing that the party still has enough ground to be a serious challenger.AAP is perhaps no longer riding the wave that brought it to power in 2022 and is now defending its record under Bhagwant Mann. Raghav Chadha's exit has also added to the churn in the party.The BJP and the Akalis are still on the margins of the state’s politics. But the scenario could change very fast. The BJP is going all out to broaden its organisational base and rope in leaders from other parties. There are also reports of talks between the BJP and the Akalis to revive their old alliance. The Congress needs to remember that the BJP is coming off a massive victory in West Bengal and is looking to expand its footprint in Punjab as well.Pilot has already made it clear that he sees Punjab as a comeback opportunity for the Congress. On Monday, he said he was confident that with a strong organisation, collective effort and the energy of party workers, Congress could return to power in the state.Pilot has the experience of being a part of successful strategising in Himachal Pradesh in the previous assembly polls and has also been a senior observer for the Kerala polls, where Congress returned to power after a decade.If Pilot can manage to bring the rival Punjab camps together and help the Congress put up a strong show in 2027, it will add to his standing within the party at a time when Rajasthan is already looking ahead to the 2028 assembly election.There has long been speculation over a bigger role for Pilot in Rajasthan. He may not have got it yet, but a successful Punjab stint could considerably strengthen his case.For a leader who has had to rebuild his own position in the party before, Punjab could well become the next big step in that comeback.
Article Summary: Congress has handed Sachin Pilot a familiar problem and a bigger opportunity. Pilot has seen enough internal wars to know how quickly a fight over one post can turn into a larger battle over leadership, political space and, of course, eventually the chief minister's chair.

MUMBAI: PM Narendra Modi Tuesday called for India to set its own standards and protocols for cross-border payments and directly integrate its payment system with countries where Indian diaspora populations are large and trade volumes significant.He said India now had a sovereign alternative to the foreign standards under-pinning the existing card-payment architecture and could connect it with the global financial system.Modi said the move could also reduce the cost of remittances, noting that Indians abroad send the largest volume of money home globally but lose a notable portion to transaction fees. “UPI can deliver substantial savings here as well, allowing funds to reach Indian families far more rapidly,” he said.His remarks came ahead of the Brics summit, where expanding national and local currency trade is a priority. A proposal seeks to enable retail and trade-settlement interoperability between fast-payment systems by linking UPI with similar networks in other countries. India has been looking at ways to reduce reliance on the dollar for cross-currency trade while Brics has stopped short of referring to the dollar, with the 2025 declaration calling for finding “acceptable mechanisms of financing in local currencies”.“We have already accomplished this with Singapore. As a result, cross-border transactions between India and Singapore occur as seamlessly as transfers between two neighbourhoods of the same city. We must replicate these integrations across other countries and international markets,” the PM said.Addressing Global Fintech Fest for the third consecutive year, Modi said India had gr-own 7.8% despite pressure on energy and commodity supply chains and escalating trade tensions. He also cited a Japanese ratings agency upgrading India to the A category, a milestone achieved after three decades. “This reflects how confident the world has become in the structural reforms implemented over the past years. And I reiterate: India’s ‘Reform Express’ will advance at an even faster pace,” he said.The PM called for stronger cybersecurity, industry-led ethical data-protection stand-ards, a regulatory-industry innovation ecosystem and a fintech consumer-protection index with clear and transparent ratings. He also said the sector needed to diversify beyond payments by expanding credit, insurance, savings, investments and pension products.Noting that Global Fintech Fest coincided with UPI’s 10th anniversary, Modi said those excluded from formal banking for generations were now driving fintech growth.He said SVANidhi credit cards had brought street vendors into the formal credit system by giving them a verifiable tool for access. Studies, he said, showed average annual income among PM SVANidhi beneficiaries had risen by over 20%.Noting that besides fintech energy, Mumbai’s cultural energy was also at its peak thanks to Ganeshotsav festivities around the corner, Modi extended warm wishes. Article Title: Village head's appeal drove Ladakh LG's initiative to tap 90 million litres of glacial water for irrigation
Article Text:
Village head’s appeal drove Ladakh LG’s initiative to tap 90 million litres of glacial water for irrigation

SRINAGAR: Nearly 90 million litres of glacial water have started irrigating more than 1,000 acres of parched farmlands across 12 villages in Ladakh every day, thanks to a pioneering initiative by lieutenant governor (LG) V K Saxena last month.The massive volume of glacier-melt, previously flowing untapped into the River Indus, is now being channelised from Stok village nallah in Leh into the Igoo-Phey Irrigation Canal using simple earthwork that incurred little capital expenditure.It was an appeal from a village chief that drove the LG to brainstorm on harnessing glaciers and snowmelt for productive use. According to officials, Saxena was on a visit to Chuchot village in Leh where the ‘goba’ (or nambardar, the traditional village head), Mirza Hussain, sought his intervention to address the acute water shortage in the village.The plea prompted the LG to spearhead a comprehensive and systematic campaign to identify locations where large volumes of glacial water were flowing down unused, draining straight into the Indus, even as surrounding farmlands remained dry, officials said.The govt first identified Stok village nallah, fed by the Stok Kangri Glacier, as one such place where glacier water could be diverted into the existing canal.Officials said the discharge from Stok nallah was assessed at 36 cusecs, or approximately 90 million litres of water in 24 hours.Two channels were then created to divert nearly 80 million litres of water into the Igoo-Phey Canal — 62 million litres toward Igoo village upstream and approximately 18 million litres toward Phey village downstream.This daily flow has substantially augmented the total water flow in the Igoo-Phey Canal — from 50 cusecs to nearly 90 cusecs. As a result, water supply will be guaranteed daily to the 12 villages fed by the canal. Previously, water from the 43-km-long Igoo-Phey Canal was distributed to villages on a restrictive roster basis due to limited availability.Having successfully channelised 80 million litres of water into the Igoo-Phey Canal, the remaining 10 million litres were diverted into another dry canal at Chuchot, and will help irrigate farmland in and around the village, officials said.“The entire 90 million litres of water was tapped and the discharge from Stok Kangri glacier into the Indus River was reduced to zero in just two days at no cost,” said an official, adding that the success of the initiative serves as a blueprint for water management across the Union Territory.
Article Summary: Nearly 90 million litres of glacial water have started irrigating more than 1,000 acres of parched farmlands across 12 villages in Ladakh every day. The massive volume of glacier-melt is now being channelised from Stok village nallah in Leh into the Igoo-Phey Irrigation Canal.

Not because the Ipsos Education Monitor survey mirrors the plot of the Shah Rukh Khan-Juhi Chawla film, but because the title neatly captures the contradiction in its India findings. Indians may believe better opportunities for growth and prosperity lie offshore, yet they remain remarkably bullish about their education system, their degrees and, above all, the future of their youth.More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. And Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value. However, ironically, 76% of Indian respondents say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad.For some parameters, TOI looked at the subset of India’s position among the 16 individual G20 member countries included in the 31-country Ipsos survey. China, Russia and Saudi Arabia were not surveyed. The survey covered 23,537 online adults across the 31 countries between June and July 2026, with about 1,000 respondents in India.Ipsos in its methodology has cautioned that its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and should be interpreted as reflecting the views of the country’s more “connected” segment.The 31-country average is an unweighted average of country results; it is not adjusted for the population size of each country.The first question was straightforward. How do people rate the overall quality of their country’s education system? In India, 51% called it good. Among the G20 countries covered by the survey, only Australia was higher, at 53%. The 31-country average was 33%. But that 51% is a number in retreat. India was at 65% in 2025, 69% in 2024 and 55% in 2023. The 14-point fall from 2025 is the steepest year-on-year decline among countries with comparable 2025 data.The contrast with several richer economies is sharp. Britain was at 43%, the US and Brazil at 32%, Italy at 29%, Japan at 24%, while France and Germany were both at 17%. That does not mean India has a better-performing education system than advanced economies. This is a matter of perception. And on that measure, Indians appear unusually confident. Just less than before.The gap becomes even more striking when the question shifts from institutions to the people coming out of them. Asked whether young people in their country have a bright future, 72% of Indian respondents agreed. That was not merely the highest figure among the G20 countries covered. It was the highest among all 31 countries surveyed. The 31-country average was 45%.Within the surveyed G20 set, Australia and South Africa were next at 54%, followed by Mexico at 52% and Canada at 50%. France was at 22%. It is perhaps one of the strongest votes of confidence in the survey. Indians appear to have placed enormous hope in their youth to put the country on the right track and take it forward.One of the hallmarks of an aspirational society like India is the belief in accumulating wealth and opportunity across generations. People believe that the hard work of one generation will make the lives of those that follow smoother. That belief gets backed in this survey. Three-fourths of Indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents. The 31-country average is 48%.Indians are also optimistic about people escaping the poverty trap. 64% believe young people from poorer backgrounds have a bright future, compared with a 31-country average of 40%. India is the highest among the G20 countries covered on both measures. And 69% of Indian respondents believe the education system contributes to reducing social inequalities, again the highest among the surveyed G20 countries. That figure is also below earlier readings, 72% in 2024 and 79% in 2023.Together, these numbers suggest that Indian respondents continue to see education as a vehicle for upward social mobility. That belief becomes even clearer when the survey turns to higher education. NITI Aayog ’s recent report also points to the continuing pull of degree programmes, noting that vocational pathways are often not seen as credible, growth-oriented alternatives and that degrees can become the safer choice amid limited counselling, social bias and low trust in existing skill systems. The Ipsos survey, albeit with a more urban and connected Indian sample, points in a similar direction. 75% of Indian respondents say a college or university degree is very important to succeed in life. 78% believe it helps people go further in their careers. And 70% say degrees in their country offer good value for money.On the first measure, India is the highest among the G20 countries surveyed. On both the other measures, it ranks second. The contrast with several advanced economies is large. On whether a degree is good value for money, India’s 70% compares with 38% in the US, 41% in Germany, 30% in Japan and 28% in Britain. Ipsos itself finds a strong positive relationship across countries between believing that a degree helps a career and believing that it offers value for money.Here again, the Ipsos study broadly aligns with a concern flagged in NITI Aayog’s skilling report that education and credentials do not automatically translate into the skills and pathways that the labour market demands. The Ipsos survey shows a deep-seated faith in formal education and yet a growing realisation that job-market demands are at times different from what is being taught in the classroom.Asked whether the school curriculum adequately prepares students for future careers, 67% of Indians agree, the highest share among the G20 countries covered by the survey. Even here, the direction has been downward: 74% agreed in 2024, 72% in 2025 and 67% now.Yet in another question on the greatest challenges facing young people, 36% of Indian respondents select “education and training systems not matching labour market demands”. That too is the highest among the G20 countries in the survey.India again falls on one extreme of a scatter plot for its two seemingly contradictory sets of beliefs. On one hand, 72% say young people have a bright future. On the other hand, 76% say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad. The 31-country average on that question is 62%.Indonesia and South Africa are even more likely to say opportunities are better overseas, at 87% and 80% respectively. Italy is at 79%. Romania matches India at 76%. But none combines that level of outward-looking aspiration with India’s exceptional optimism about the future of its young.This is perhaps the central finding of the entire report for India. Respondents may be optimistic about India’s young people precisely because they believe those young people possess education and skills that give them more options, including the option of leaving. The optimism may be about the people. The doubt may be about the location of opportunity.The dichotomy in the approach of Indians extends to technology too. 78% support banning social media for children under 14, both inside and outside school. The 31-country average is 73%.Support has climbed 10 points in a year. India was at 68% in 2025 and 73% in 2024.On smartphones, 57% of Indian respondents favour a ban in schools, exactly matching the 31-country average. That is up from 50% last year and 52% in 2024. But attitudes to AI are different.Only 26% of Indian respondents say AI, including ChatGPT, should be banned in schools, compared with 39% across the 31 countries. Indian opinion on AI has moved sharply over the four editions of the survey. 39% wanted AI banned in schools in both 2025 and 2024, compared with just 16% in 2023. The 13-point drop from 2025 to 2026 is the largest year-on-year fall among countries with comparable 2025 data.Britain, the US and Poland moved in the other direction, rising to 52%, 56% and 46%, respectively.To sum up, India’s ‘connected’ population has not lost faith in education. Quite the opposite. It remains unusually convinced that education matters, degrees pay, children can surpass their parents and those from poorer homes can climb. What appears less certain is where that promise will ultimately be realised.andmay finally be different. That is the sobering realisation one can derive from this survey.
Article Summary: More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value.

Article Title: India, China hold first high-level military flag talks in Arunachal amid LAC tensions
Article Text:
India, China hold first high-level military flag meeting in Arunachal sector

New military mechanism along eastern frontier

Border peace remains key to improving ties

Military engagement ahead of Xi visit

NEW DELHI: India and China have held their first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting in the Arunachal Pradesh sector, with talks taking place on both sides of the frontier earlier this week.The meeting followed understandings reached during the Special Representatives dialogue between National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi. The talks are part of efforts by the two countries to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and gradually improve bilateral ties.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side on September 6 and at Damai on the Chinese side on September 7.Jaiswal said the meeting followed agreements reached during the Special Representatives talks in August 2025 and August 2026, along with subsequent discussions under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination."Pursuant to the understandings reached between the Special Representatives of India and China in August 2025 and August 2026, and subsequent discussions at the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination meetings held in Beijing and New Delhi in May and August 2026 respectively, the first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side in Arunachal Pradesh on September 6 and Damai on the Chinese side on September 7," Jaiswal said at his weekly media briefing."A similar mechanism also exists in the Western Sector," he said.The talks took place amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.Jaiswal also said that India-China relations are gradually moving in a "positive direction".Doval and Wang, who are the designated Special Representatives for the India-China boundary talks, held their latest dialogue in Beijing last month.During the meeting, the two sides discussed the delimitation of the boundary, trans-boundary cooperation and the need to maintain peace along the LAC.The Indian side stressed that peace and tranquillity along the border are important for the continued development of bilateral relations.The Special Representatives mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which covers a 3,488-km frontier.India and China have taken several steps in recent months to rebuild relations that deteriorated sharply after the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. The latest military engagement comes days before Chinese president Xi Jinping is expected to visit India for the BRICS summit. Xi is likely to arrive in New Delhi on Saturday.
Article Summary: India, China hold first high-level military flag meeting in Arunachal sector. Talks are part of efforts by the two countries to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) The latest military engagement comes days before Chinese president Xi Jinping is expected to visit India.

Article Title: 'You can't keep it lingering': Supreme Court to Odisha on Dara Singh plea

Article Title: No rooms, Rs 2.3 lakh a night: BRICS Summit sends Delhi hotel rates soaring

NEW DELHI: As India prepares to host the 18th BRICS Leaders’ Summit, luxury hotels in the national capital are facing a sharp squeeze in room availability, with tariffs at some marquee properties climbing beyond Rs 2 lakh a night ahead of the September 12-13 gathering.The summit, which brings leaders of the expanded BRICS grouping to Delhi and marks two decades since the bloc’s founding, is driving concentrated demand for high-end accommodation, with several premium hotels showing limited or no availability and others quoting rates of more than Rs 2 lakh per night, according to news agency PTI.Booking checks showed no room availability at Taj Mahal and The Oberoi in New Delhi for September 11-12, while Taj Palace had no rooms available for September 10-12. The Leela Palace, New Delhi, was also not accepting bookings for stays between September 10 and 12.At ITC Maurya, New Delhi, rooms available for September 10-13 were commanding tariffs starting at more than Rs 2.3 lakh a night.The surge comes as delegates and other visitors are expected to arrive in the capital ahead of the two-day summit and extend their stays, putting pressure on room inventory, particularly in central Delhi.K B Kachru, president, Hotel Association of India (HAI) and Chairman - South Asia, Radisson Hotel Group, said the summit was highlighting the pressure on India's hospitality infrastructure."India is commanding global attention at a defining moment -- as the nation prepares to host marquee international events and cements its position as a premier MICE destination, the world is watching how we scale to meet our tourism targets."The BRICS Summit alone will put considerable focus on room inventory and that spotlight is exposing a hard truth: our hospitality infrastructure has not kept pace with our tourism ambition," he said, according to PTI.Kachru said India currently has only about 200,000-220,000 branded hotel rooms, which he described as inadequate for the country's tourism ambitions.The demand is also being felt beyond central Delhi. Rahool Macarius, Market Managing Director, Eurasia, Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, said the summit was creating a distinct demand pattern across Delhi-NCR."At Ramada Encore by Wyndham, Dwarka Expressway, this event-led demand is reflected in occupancy for September 12-15, currently tracking at 65 per cent, significantly ahead of the broader market demand," he said.For tourists, business travellers and families visiting Delhi during the period, the squeeze could mean higher accommodation costs or a shift towards hotels outside central areas and lower-priced properties.However, hotel tariffs and availability remain dynamic and can change with bookings, cancellations and fresh inventory releases. Emails seeking comments from the hotels cited for availability and tariffs remained unanswered till the time of publication, PTI reported.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 5 crore with its Registry by Wednesday as a condition for exempting him from surrendering to serve his sentence in a cheque-bounce case involving film producer-financier Murli Projects Pvt Ltd.A bench headed by the Chief Justice, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, passed the order after Yadav’s plea was orally mentioned before it, as cited by ANI.The court issued a conditional notice on Yadav’s plea challenging the Delhi High Court’s July 10 judgment upholding his conviction and three-month imprisonment in seven cases under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.The matter will next be heard on September 15.The Delhi high court had earlier directed Yadav to surrender and serve his sentence by September 10 after dismissing his criminal revision petitions challenging his conviction and sentence.The case stems from seven complaints filed by Murli Projects against Yadav, his wife Radha Rajpal Yadav and their film production company over the dishonour of seven cheques issued in connection with financing for the film Ata Pata Lapata.According to the case records, Murli Projects advanced Rs 5 crore in 2010 for completion of the film. As the film’s release was delayed, the parties subsequently entered into a series of agreements, with the repayment amount revised at different stages.Yadav’s petition states that the original transaction was an investment in the film rather than a loan, and that the cheques were issued as security. Under a third supplementary agreement signed in August 2012, eight post-dated cheques were issued, with the repayment obligation linked to the film’s release.The dispute escalated after Murli Projects approached the Delhi High Court in 2012 over the film and obtained an order restraining the petitioners from creating third-party interests in its rights. Subsequently, seven complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act were filed over the dishonour of seven cheques.The petitioners, however, rely on a subsequent consent agreement dated April 21, 2013, under which the parties agreed to a full and final settlement of Rs 10.40 crore, including Rs 40 lakh already paid through RTGS.Four fresh post-dated cheques were issued to secure the settlement. Yadav’s plea says the agreement required the earlier eight security cheques to be returned, but Murli Projects instead proceeded with the dishonoured-cheque cases.The trial court convicted Yadav and the other accused in April 2018 in all seven complaints. Yadav was initially sentenced to six months’ imprisonment and fined Rs 1.60 crore in each case.The sentence was later reduced. On May 22, 2019, he was sentenced to three months’ simple imprisonment and fined Rs 1.35 crore in each of the seven cases, with the sentences to run concurrently.

Article Title: The ‘veg-only’ gatekeepers of urban housing in India
Article Text:
A real estate agent posted a video promoting a high-value flat in Tardeo — priced at around Rs 6.5 crore — attached to a ‘veg-only’ condition. The clip went viral, then triggered criticism from political parties and social media users, after which the agent apologised.

Food, friction… flashpoints

Changing localities

The insidious veg ‘logic’

Societies’ gatekeepers

The legal angle

Pan-India phenomenon

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(With inputs from Sudipto Das & Sunny Baski)

Shreepati Arcade at Nana Chowk, south Mumbai, entered the city’s imagination in 2002 as an engineering and real-estate milestone: at 45 floors and around 161 metres, it was then the tallest occupied residential tower in India. Yet, the detail that has outlasted the height record is not architectural. It is social. The tower’s developer, R C Chaturvedi, has said that the apartments were sold only to vegetarian families, primarily from Jain, Marwari, and Sindhi communities, and that a handful of interested non-vegetarian buyers from a minority community were asked to step aside in the name of establishing a “vegetarian society”.“It became the USP for selling the flats,” recollects Chaturvedi. “We realised that most of the clients showing interest were vegetarians. There were only four clients from a minority community, all non-vegetarians, who were keen to buy the apartments in the tower. But we requested them and explained to them that this would be a vegetarian society. They respected our decision.”More than two decades later, the building’s identity as a veg-only zone remains intact. The story is not so much an aberration as an example of a longrunning Mumbai pattern: housing societies and neighbourhoods as spaces where personal preference, community power, and public claims of equality are continually negotiated, and often contested.Few issues make that friction as visible as food. Vegetarianism can be a matter of individual taste, but in many communities, it is also a marker of ritual practice and group identity. In Mumbai’s property market, it has periodically become a screening device — sometimes openly stated, sometimes silently enforced — determining who can live where, and at what cost.A recent controversy illustrates how contemporary marketing can amplify an old practice. A real estate agent posted a video promoting a high-value flat in Tardeo — priced at around Rs 6.5 crore — attached to a ‘veg-only’ condition. The clip went viral, then triggered criticism from political parties and social media users, after which the agent apologised. The speed of the backlash made the episode seem like a new flashpoint, but property market observers know how veg-only buildings, and clusters have existed for decades. The difference today is that the condition is more easily recorded, shared, and debated publicly, rather than remaining an informal understanding between brokers and resident committees.Mumbai’s “vegetarian clusters” have historical roots that are partly demographic and partly economic. Localities like Walkeshwar and Babulnath in south Mumbai, and parts of Ghatkopar on the eastern suburbs are often cited as areas where communities observing strict vegetarianism have consolidated over time.Upscale South Mumbai areas of Walkeshwar and Nepean Sea Road are even said to have no non-veg restaurants anywhere. Jashwant Mehta, a Walkeshwar resident, said some housing societies there have Jain temples and are home only to vegetarians. “In fact, demand and prices in such societies are higher than in buildings with better amenities,” he said.A Malabar Hill resident said that in some housing societies, where the majority is vegetarian, it is informally understood that the sale of flats is only to vegetarian families. “However, such conditions are not put in writing. This practice is prevalent in many areas of Mumbai,” the resident said.Some of this clustering followed familiar urban patterns: groups migrated for trade and employment, relied on community networks for housing and finance, and preferred to live near places of worship and businesses aligned with their customs. Once a neighbourhood acquired a reputation — whether for Jain temples, specific festival calendars, or food norms — successive waves of residents reinforced the same identity, making it harder for outsiders to enter even without any explicit written rule.Notably, the practice is not limited to enclaves stereotyped as ‘Gujarati’ or ‘Jain’. Even traditionally Marathi stronghold areas like Dadar, Lalbaug, and Kalachowki have housing projects that cater exclusively to vegetarian communities.There are multiple motives behind insisting on vegetarian-only residency, and they do not all carry the same weight. Some residents argue from the standpoint of religious discipline, ritual purity, and sensory comfort: they do not want the smell of meat in corridors, the possibility of cooking odours entering ventilation shafts, or shared spaces being used for non-vegetarian catering. Others frame it as a lifestyle choice akin to rules about noise, pets, or smoking. In this view, a building is shared environment, and residents can seek neighbours with compatible habits.But the same rule can also operate as a proxy for excluding particular communities. A property agent said vegetarianism is sometimes insisted upon to keep out members of minority communities, many of whom are presumed to be meat-eaters.The conflict sharpens in buildings with shared facilities, because common spaces force residents to negotiate collective norms. Many larger complexes now include community halls, clubhouses, banquet spaces, and sometimes society-run cafeterias or in-house restaurants. Architect Moayyed Fatehi describes a common arrangement: a residential complex may be multicommunal and harmonious on the surface, yet impose parameters on food in shared spaces.Fatehi’s own example from a luxury complex in Worli, Central Mumbai, indicates how these rules can be designed as a compromise: residents are free to cook and eat what they like inside their private flats, but society-controlled kitchens and banquet facilities remain veg-only. “Non-veg food cannot be cooked in the common banquet hall, but it can be served if you get it from outside,” he said.Developers, too, play a role in shaping these norms. Many do not impose strict dietary restrictions, because it narrows the buyer pool and complicates sales. Yet, reports suggest some have begun reserving one wing or a couple of floors within a larger complex for vegetarians, a move that transforms social preference into a physical partition.Brokers and agents become key intermediaries in this ecosystem, because they accumulate informal knowledge about which buildings will reject which buyers. Over time, many learn to pre-filter enquiries. If they believe a society will object to minority communities, single women, bachelors, or openly nonvegetarian tenants, they may avoid showing those listings to those clients in the first place. This creates a parallel property market, where the burden falls on excluded groups: higher search costs, repeated rejections, more time spent negotiating, and sometimes a “minority premium” in the form of higher rents or prices in the smaller set of buildings willing to accept them.The legal picture remains contested. One approach, said housinglaw specialists like advocate Anil Harish, treats a housing society as an association of like-minded members. Under this reasoning, people may choose to contract with those who share their norms, and a society may regulate collective life much as it might regulate commercial use of apartments, structural alterations, or other activities affecting neighbours. From that vantage point, a vegetarian-only condition is defended as an expression of freedom of association and contractual choice.The opposing approach holds that cooperative housing societies are not purely private clubs; they are quasi-public institutions managing essential urban resources — housing and neighbourhood access — within a framework meant to be open and non-discriminatory.A 2005 Supreme Court judgment — Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd vs District Registrar, Cooperative Societies (Urban) — is the leading case on the issue. The Zoroastrian Society bylaws restricting membership exclusively to members of the Parsi community, was challenged when a Parsi member sought to transfer his plot to a non-Parsi builder. “The apex court reversed the lower court order and upheld the validity of the society’s by-law. It held that there was nothing in the Gujarat Cooperative Societies Act, 1961 or Rules that precluded a society from restricting membership to persons of a particular community, persuasion or belief. The society’s “community-based membership restriction was upheld”, and the attempt to force admission/transfer contrary to the bylaws did not succeed.But advocate Vinod Sampat has argued that open membership is foundational: societies cannot discriminate on grounds of caste, creed, religion, or sex, and restrictions that prevent someone from buying a flat violate fundamental rights tied to residence and equality. “Article 15 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination by the state, and arbitrary exclusion by private bodies/societies violating public policy,” he said.“A housing society’s role is strictly administrative, limited to clearing dues and recording transfers. They cannot superimpose discriminatory rules or reject valid sale deeds,” Sampat pointed out, adding that many restrictions imposed by office-bearers amount to an abuse of power. This argument treats discriminatory gatekeeping as an unlawful barrier to equal participation in city life.Veg-only societies span regions and cities, reinforced by kinship and community ties and promoted by a preference for dietary common ground among neighbours. So, in Kolkata, with its love of machher jhol and kosha mangsho, several buildings and societies have quietly remained as vegetarian enclaves, shaped largely by Gujarati, Jain and Marwari communities. In South Kolkata’s Bhowanipore, the constituency now represented by CM Suvendu Adhikari and formerly by ex-CM Mamata Banerjee, the coming together of veg-only societies occurred over the decades.Till the mid-20th century, Bhowanipore was mainly an upper-middle class Bengali neighbourhood with a sizeable Sikh presence. Decades of migration and clustering have made veg-only societies a common feature so much so that some properties in Bhowanipore are sold or rented only to families that follow a strict vegetarian diet.Same is the story in Hyderabad. Cosmopolitan on the outside, conservative in pockets, the Telangana capital is well used to landlords in some traditional neighbourhoods preferring to rent out their homes only to vegetarian tenants.While Hyderabad’s western corridor, particularly Gachibowli, Hi-tech city, Kondapur, Nallagandal and Tellapur, has a relatively fluid rental market where food habits rarely become a major consideration, the situation is different in older neighbourhoods like Lingampally in Kacheguda, Chikkadpally, Badichowdi, Gujarati Galli, Gowliguda, Chappal Bazaar, etc.“Our main objective is to keep our property clean and maintain its sanctity. We do not want nonvegetarian food to affect the atmosphere or purity of our home. Ultimately, we give the property based on trust, as we cannot keep monitoring what tenants buy, order or bring into the house,” said a landlord in Chikkadpally.So, Shreepati Arcade’s veg-only identity — once marketed as a unique selling proposition — now sits within a larger story: a reminder that a city’s skyline does not just reflect wealth and engineering, but also the boundaries — sometimes visible, often invisible — that residents draw around belonging.
Article Summary: Mumbai’s ‘vegetarian clusters’ have historical roots that are partly demographic and partly economic. Localities like Walkeshwar and Babulnath in south Mumbai and parts of Ghatkopar are often cited as areas where communities observing strict vegetarianism have consolidated over time.

Article Title: Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit
Article Text:
Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit

India for Brics

Key challenges for India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India will host the annual Brics summit on Sept 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At Brics, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies - Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, the UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia - along with 10 other partner countries.The theme of India's 2026 chairship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability', drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to Brics. Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level, including the foreign ministers' and national security advisers' engagements.Despite political fragmentation and economic imbalances, Brics remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world.It reinforces India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reaffirms an independent foreign policy.Brics also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to Brics is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to shape the agenda of the developing world. India's moderating influence prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus too on expanding financial architecture, as no govt would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it cannot control. As foreign minister S Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency.Brics also provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. Brics' membership deepens India's trade ties with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from over-reliance on any single partner.The first, of course, is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint Brics declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India will likely focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ring-fence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on US currency. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement while maintaining it is against any common Brics currency or China-centred replacement mechanism.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about Brics' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's economic agenda, India avoided endorsing SCO's 2030 economic roadmap, and it must work with Beijing in Brics on shared objectives, though without letting the forum become a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing.Jaishankar said while announcing the summit that Brics must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit, with key deliverables like a unanimous Brics declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.To conclude, inclusion of African Union was not the only major takeaway from 2023's G20 summit. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, which allowed a G20 declaration. India can derive confidence from that diplomatic triumph as it heads into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.
Article Summary: India will host the annual Brics summit on Sept 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. The theme of India's 2026 chairship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability', drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' approach to Brics.
